hook.line: Mariana is about to print a story about the block, and her editor asks: are you sure, or do you only think so? Spanish has a firm way to say "I have no doubt" and another for "I know it for a fact".
hook.es: No me cabe la menor duda de que Vale tiene razón.
hook.en: I haven't the slightest doubt that Vale is right.

examples.es: No me cabe la menor duda de que Vale tiene razón.
examples.en: I haven't the slightest doubt that Vale is right.

examples.es: Me consta que Hernando pagó la cuenta.
examples.en: I know for a fact that Hernando paid the bill.

examples.es: No me cabe duda de que vendrá.
examples.en: I have no doubt that he will come.

examples.es: Me consta que le avisaron ayer.
examples.en: I know for a fact that they told him yesterday.
Do you know for a fact that they signed the contract? (to a friend)

examples.es: No nos cabe duda de que ganaremos.
examples.en: We have no doubt that we will win.

rule:
*No me cabe la menor duda de que* means "I have no doubt that". *Me consta que* means "I know for a fact that", because I have seen the proof.

Both are followed by the plain verb: *tiene*, *pagó*, *vendrá*. You are sure, so there is no wish form.

They work like *me gusta*: the doubt or the fact is the subject, and you are *me*. For other people, change it: *no nos cabe duda*, *te consta*, *le consta*.

English just says "I'm sure". These two are heavier and more formal, the voice of a witness.
smallPrint: Teachers call these expressions of certainty, and *me consta* in particular carries evidence behind it.

readAndPick.es: No nos cabe duda de que ganaremos.
options: We have no doubt that we will win.
I have no doubt that I will win.
They have no doubt that they will win.

readAndPick.es: Me consta que Hernando pagó la cuenta.
options: I know for a fact that Hernando will pay the bill.
I know for a fact that Hernando paid the bill.
I know for a fact that Hernando is paying the bill.
Do I know for a fact that they signed the contract?
Do you know for a fact that they will sign the contract?
Do you know for a fact that they signed the contract?

readAndPick.es: No me cabe duda de que vendrá.
options: I have no doubt that he will come.
I have no doubt that he came.
I doubt that he will come.

readAndPick.es: A Hernando le consta que Rosa trabajó aquí cuarenta años.
options: We know for a fact that Rosa worked here forty years.
I know for a fact that Rosa worked here forty years.
Hernando knows for a fact that Rosa worked here forty years.

readAndPick.es: Me consta que le avisaron ayer.
options: I know for a fact that he told them yesterday.
I know for a fact that they told him yesterday.
I know for a fact that I told him yesterday.

readAndPick.es: No me cabe la menor duda de que Vale tiene razón.
options: Vale has no doubt that I am right.
I am not sure that Vale is right.
I have no doubt at all that Vale is right.

readAndPick.es: Me consta que ella no firmó nada.
options: I know for a fact that she signed nothing.
I know for a fact that she will sign something.
I am not sure that she signed anything.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *No me cabe duda de que Vale ___ razón.* (*tiene* or *tenga*) I have no doubt that Vale is right.
yourTurn.answer: No me cabe duda de que Vale tiene razón.
yourTurn.why: You are sure, so the verb stays plain: *tiene*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Me consta que Hernando ___ la cuenta.* (*pagó* or *pagará*) I know for a fact that Hernando paid the bill.
yourTurn.answer: Me consta que Hernando pagó la cuenta.
yourTurn.why: A fact you know about something already done needs the past: *pagó*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I know for a fact that they told him yesterday.
yourTurn.answer: Me consta que le avisaron ayer.
accept: Me consta que ayer le avisaron.
yourTurn.why: *Me consta que* opens the sentence, and the rest is a plain statement.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: We have no doubt that we will win.
yourTurn.answer: No nos cabe duda de que ganaremos.
accept: No nos cabe la menor duda de que ganaremos.
yourTurn.why: *Nos* replaces *me* because the doubt belongs to all of us.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: Do you know for a fact that they signed the contract?
yourTurn.why: For a friend you swap *me* for *te*: *¿te consta?*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Me consta que ella firmó algo.* (I know for a fact that she signed nothing)
yourTurn.answer: Me consta que ella no firmó nada.
yourTurn.why: In a negative sentence *algo* turns into *nada*, and *no* goes in front of the verb; *me consta* stays the same.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Hernando knows for a fact that Rosa worked here forty years.
yourTurn.answer: A Hernando le consta que Rosa trabajó aquí cuarenta años.
accept: Le consta a Hernando que Rosa trabajó aquí cuarenta años.
yourTurn.why: For another person you use *le*, and *a Hernando* names who it is.

pitfalls.wrong: No me cabe duda de que Vale tenga razón.
pitfalls.right: No me cabe duda de que Vale tiene razón.
pitfalls.why: Almost. You have no doubt, so the verb stays plain; the wish form is for when you do doubt.

pitfalls.wrong: No me cabe duda que Vale tiene razón.
pitfalls.right: No me cabe duda de que Vale tiene razón.
pitfalls.why: Almost. After *duda* Spanish keeps the *de* in front of *que*.

pitfalls.wrong: Yo consto que Hernando pagó la cuenta.
pitfalls.right: Me consta que Hernando pagó la cuenta.
pitfalls.why: Almost. The fact is what is "clear" to you, so you are *me*, like in *me gusta*.

personal: Write one thing you know for a fact about your own neighbourhood, starting with *Me consta que*, and one thing you have no doubt about, starting with *No me cabe duda de que*.
